articles.title: Understanding Closures in JavaScript
articles.subtitle: All you need to know abount closures in JS

blocks.title: Begining
paragraphs: Closures are a powerful but often misunderstood feature in JavaScript. At their core, a closure is when an inner function has access to variables from its outer (enclosing) function, even after the outer function has finished executing. This happens because functions in JS 'remember' their lexical scope.

blocks.title: Why Do Closures Matter?
paragraphs: Closures let you create private variables, maintain state without global pollution, and build modular code. They're key for patterns like modules, event handlers, and callbacks.

blocks.title: Simple Example
paragraphs: Consider this classic counter:

Here, createCounter returns an inner function. Even after createCounter finishes, the inner function 'closes over' count, keeping it alive and private. Trying to access count from outside fails—true encapsulation!

blocks.title: Real-World Use: Event Listeners
paragraphs: Closures shine in loops with events:
Using let (block-scoped) creates a new i for each iteration, avoiding the classic var bug where all buttons alert 'Button 3'.

blocks.title: Common Pitfall
paragraphs: Memory leaks! Closures hold references, so remove event listeners in long-lived apps to free memory.
Closures make JS functional and flexible—master them, and your code will feel more elegant.

articles.title: Docker Fundamentals: Containerize Your Apps
articles.subtitle: From images to orchestration – everything you need to get started

blocks.title: What is Docker?
paragraphs: Docker is a platform that uses OS-level virtualization to deliver software in packages called containers. Containers bundle your app with its dependencies, ensuring it runs identically anywhere – from dev laptop to production cloud.

blocks.title: Why Docker Revolutionized Development?
paragraphs: Solves 'it works on my machine' issues. Lightweight (vs VMs), fast startup, portable across Linux/Mac/Windows. Enables microservices, CI/CD, and consistent environments.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
paragraphs: Image: Read-only template (like a snapshot). Container: Running instance of an image. Dockerfile: Script to build images. Registry: Storage for images (Docker Hub is public default).

blocks.title: Install and Run Your First Container
paragraphs: Install Docker Desktop (docker.com). Pull and run Nginx:

blocks.code:
docker pull nginx

docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name my-nginx nginx

# Visit localhost:8080 → Nginx welcome page!

# Stop and remove
docker stop my-nginx
docker rm my-nginx

paragraphs: `-d` runs detached, `-p` maps ports, `--name` labels it. Boom – web server in seconds!

blocks.title: Build Your Own Image with Dockerfile
paragraphs: Create a simple Node.js app container:
`FROM` base image, `RUN` executes commands, `CMD` default run. Build creates layers for efficiency.

blocks.title: Volumes for Persistent Data
paragraphs: Containers are ephemeral – use volumes for data:

blocks.code:
docker run -d -p 5432:5432 -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data --name db postgres

# Named volume 'pgdata' persists outside container

paragraphs: List: `docker volume ls`. Great for databases.

blocks.title: Docker Compose for Multi-Container Apps
paragraphs: Orchestrate services with docker-compose.yml:

blocks.code:
version: '3.8'
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  pgdata:

# Run: docker-compose up

paragraphs: Defines networks, scaling, env vars. Perfect for full-stack apps.

blocks.title: Essential Commands and Best Practices
paragraphs: Key commands: `docker ps/a` (list), `docker logs <name>`, `docker exec -it <name> /bin/sh` (shell).
Tips: Use `.dockerignore`, multi-stage builds for smaller images, non-root users, scan with Trivy.

blocks.title: Next Steps
paragraphs: Explore Kubernetes for orchestration, Docker Swarm for built-in clustering. Docker makes deployment reliable – start small, scale big!
Practice on Docker Hub or Katacoda playgrounds.

articles.title: Mastering Asynchronous Programming in Python
articles.subtitle: Handling concurrency with async/await and asyncio

blocks.title: What is Asynchronous Programming?
paragraphs: Python's async programming lets your code handle I/O-bound tasks efficiently without blocking the main thread. Introduced in Python 3.5 via asyncio, it uses coroutines, event loops, and async/await syntax to run tasks concurrently.

blocks.title: Why Use Async in Python?
paragraphs: Perfect for web servers, API calls, file I/O, or database queries. It scales better than threads for I/O-heavy apps, avoiding GIL limitations while keeping code readable.

blocks.title: Basic async/await Example
paragraphs: Start with a simple coroutine that simulates network delays:

blocks.code:
import asyncio
import time

async def fetch_data(delay, name):
    print(f'Starting {name}...')
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # Non-blocking sleep
    print(f'{name} done!')
    return f'Result from {name}'

async def main():
    # Run tasks concurrently
    tasks = [
        fetch_data(2, 'API1'),
        fetch_data(1, 'API2'),
        fetch_data(3, 'API3')
    ]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())

paragraphs: This runs all fetches concurrently—total time is ~3s (max delay), not 6s sequentially. `asyncio.gather` awaits all without blocking.

blocks.title: Real-World: HTTP Requests
paragraphs: Use aiohttp for async HTTP. Fetch multiple URLs in parallel:

blocks.code:
import aiohttp
import asyncio

async def fetch_url(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        return await response.text()

async def main():
    urls = [
        'https://api.github.com',
        'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1'
    ]
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        tasks = [fetch_url(session, url) for url in urls]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
        print([len(r) for r in results])

asyncio.run(main())

paragraphs: aiohttp handles connections efficiently. Install with `pip install aiohttp`.

blocks.title: Key Tips and Pitfalls
paragraphs: Always `await` coroutines—don't call them like regular functions. Use `asyncio.run()` for top-level entry. Avoid mixing sync (e.g., `time.sleep`) with async; it blocks the event loop.
Async shines for I/O, not CPU-bound tasks (use multiprocessing for those). Frameworks like FastAPI build on this for high-performance APIs.
